newsitem.title: UK: Dlr off highs but bulls look to U.S. jobs data.
newsitem.headline: Dlr off highs but bulls look to U.S. jobs data.

text.p: The dollar pared gains from 11-week highs against the yen on Friday, but analysts said market sentiment was bullish enough to push the dollar higher if U.S. July payroll data turned out to be in line with expectations.
Dollar/yen retreated before stoploss orders near 119.25 could be triggered, dealers said. The U.S. currency was little changed below Monday's 7-1/2 year peak.
But analysts said both levels could still be breached.
"The market feels as though it has the upper hand. I think we're going to test these levels," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
Traders in dollar/yen were wary of verbal intervention from Japanese authorities to curb the dollar's rise.
An official at Japan's Ministry of Finance declined to comment on rumours that the Ministry had urged people not to buy dollars above 119 yen.
Dealers in Tokyo said they would be less cautious about testing the dollar's upside until the Finance Ministry's influential official, Eisuke Sakakibara, returned from holiday on Tuesday.
In London, a trader said: "The environment is still bullish overall. We're still looking for dollar/yen to test 120-121."
Dollar/yen stood at 118.95/9.00 at 1116 GMT compared with 118.33/38 late on Thursday.

Comments from different Japanese officials this week both criticised and played down the surging dollar/yen rate, sending mixed messages to currency markets and stoking fear that friction may resurface over the U.S./Japanese trade gap.
But the dollar clawed back ground after U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated on Thursday that a strong dollar is in the United States' best interests.
"There's been a lot of rhetoric on both sides, but we're still focusing on the upside," said the London trader.
He said despite a bout of profit-taking earlier on, dollar/yen was still bid.
"The market is essentially long of dollar and people are waiting for the U.S. figures to confirm their views," he said.
Economists forecast the data, due at 1230 GMT, to show 193,000 new jobs were added to July payrolls compared to 217,000 in June.

"The data would have to be significantly at variance with forecasts to shake what is a very firm consensus in the markets - namely, growth heading back towards trend, inflation non-existent and Fed on hold," said Meggysi at DMG.
Optimism over the dollar resurfaced on Thursday in the wake of second quarter gross domestic product figures which showed U.S. inflation was in check.
Dollar/mark traders said they expected the jobs data to be as encouraging. They saw the dollar sailing through the key 1.85 level, breaching Monday's 7-1/2 year high of 1.8490 marks.

"We're expecting the dollar to maintain its strength, push up towards this year's highs and maybe even make new ones," said a second London dealer. "Although we ultimately predict a bearish trend coming back in, short term we see dollar/mark testing 1.90."
At 1258 GMT dollar/mark was trading at 1.8483/93 versus 1.8395/405 late Thursday.
Dealers said a sharp move higher could spark some heavy selling of dollar, and would also underpin sterling/mark.
"Sterling/mark could easily get up to around 3.05 marks this afternoon if dollar/mark can break through 1.8520," said one.

The pound was boosted by Britain's Howard Davies who, ending his tenure as Bank of England governor to become head of Britain's new City regulatory body, told BBC radio on Friday, "a modest rise in interest rates may well be needed ... now or later".
But sterling later came off against the feisty dollar, with cable down at $1.6370/80 from 1.6404/14 on Thursday.
Analysts said the pound was taking a rest after its rollercoaster week, but remained fairly well supported.
"Cable is topped around 1.6425, but all depends on sterling/mark," said the London trader.
-- Catherine Bremer, London newsroom +44 171 542 7719
